summary: Avery Clarke's October 16, 2023 article describes how education and skill development are adapting to the tech industry's rapid growth. It covers STEM-heavy curricula, continuous learning and micro-credentials, tech hubs that decentralize education, the lasting value of soft skills, gig-economy skill portfolios, and initiatives for underserved communities. It concludes that educators, industry and governments must coordinate to build an adaptable workforce.
one_line: Avery Clarke's article explains how schools, employers and tech hubs are reshaping education and skills training to meet the tech economy's demands.
key_facts: The article 'Redefining Education: Preparing for Tech's Tidal Wave' was written by Avery Clarke and dated October 16, 2023.

Educational institutions, including high schools, vocational schools and universities, are integrating more STEM (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) programs to produce graduates who are 'tech natives'.
Kennedy Tech High School in Portland, described as recently refurbished and launched 'just last month', replaced traditional shop classes with coding boot camps and robotics leagues.
Amazon and Google offer certification programs, often online micro-credentials, that keep even seasoned employees current on innovation.
The Nexus Hub in Boise, Idaho, a tech incubator and accelerator, opened its doors in January 2024.
Programs at tech hubs combine hands-on tech exposure with mentorship from industry veterans, and employers help shape courses to fit their needs.
Emotional intelligence, critical thinking and creativity remain at a premium because machines cannot replicate genuine human connection and innovation.
Educators are intertwining soft skill development with technical curricula.
Jameson Locke, a contract app developer based in Seattle, works on multiple projects requiring technical skills plus project management and communication abilities.
Institutions are implementing cross-disciplinary training in response to the rise in freelance and contract work.
Code to Inspire, founded by Afghan tech entrepreneur Fereshteh Forough in late 2023, equips underrepresented groups with digital tools to overcome socioeconomic barriers.
The article says VR and AR are carving niches in training, marketing and consumer experience, and that automation and AI will take on more tasks once done by humans.
